newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's new finance critic urges tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Canada's new finance critic urges tax cuts.

text.p: The new shadow finance minister for Canada's official opposition aims to pressure the Liberal government into cutting personal and corporate taxes.

Monte Solberg, 38, a former commercial radio manager from Medicine Hat, Alberta, was named on Friday as the Reform Party's choice to face off against Canada's heavyweight Liberal Finance Minister Paul Martin in the House of Commons.

Reform replaced the secessionist Bloc Quebecois as official opposition in the June 2 federal election by winning the second most seats in Parliament. The party draws most of its support from conservative Western Canada.
Reform made tax cuts a major campaign plank.

"One of the big issues is what the government is going to do once we balance the budget," Solberg said in a telephone interview. "They've made noises about not cutting taxes, which means they're not doing the one thing that creates jobs."

Canada has the highest personal income taxes among the Group of Seven industrial nations and the fourth highest among member countries of the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development, a recent OECD study said.
The ruling Liberals have pledged to eliminate the budget deficit within two years, but have not committed to broad-based tax cuts.

Solberg urged reduced government spending and voiced concern about "noises they (Liberals) are making about new spending" after election results showed the Liberals hurt by spending cuts to slash the budget deficit in recent years.
Left-leaning Liberal legislators have pressed for increased social spending.
But Martin has vowed that the government would stay the course on deficit cutting and begin chipping away at Canada's debt mountain after the deficit was eliminated.
Martin has said the deficit for 1996-97 would likely fall below C$16 billion (11.5 billion). Canada's debt for 1997-98 was expected to total C$610.3 billion (US$438.5 billion).
